children: By Terell Wright
Students at Williams College pay less to attend on average than the in-state cost at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
Those at Grinnell College pay less than Iowans going to the University of Iowa.
And at Swarthmore College, the average student pays roughly half of what peers fork out at Penn State.

A growing group of elite liberal-arts colleges long known for eye-watering price tags is turning out to be quite the bargain for many students — and the schools want you to know it. They have been rolling out expansive financial-aid policies for families of all income levels in a bid to stand out to a shrinking pool of college applicants.

"We want families who earn $200,000, $250,000, $300,000 per year and, in some cases, more to know that they may qualify for financial aid at Swarthmore," said Varo Duffins, the college's director of financial aid.

The sticker price for attending Swarthmore is $98,370, including extra costs like transportation. But this year's average aid package is $78,118, covering roughly 80% of attendance costs. Nearly 350 of Swarthmore's roughly 1,700 students pay nothing. And starting in the next academic year, the school won't charge tuition to families with typical assets earning under $200,000.

Others including Williams College have introduced similar thresholds for covering tuition. It is a shift for the top dogs in higher education, which have long associated prestige with high tuition. Facing tighter recruitment battles, private colleges are now advertising affordability. They are expanding need-based aid widely enough to compete on price against historically cheaper alternatives, following the lead of top universities like Harvard and Princeton.
"You can often go to a small liberal-arts college cheaper than your state flagship university," said Laurie Kopp Weingarten, president and chief educational consultant at One-Stop College Counseling.

That is what Jonah Chen found. The 18-year-old chose Bowdoin College in Maine after applying to 14 schools, including three public flagships. The college offered an aid package covering almost 80% of its $97,900 first-year cost, leaving him to pay $21,000. At the University of Maryland, College Park, his local public university, he would have paid the full in-state cost of $32,408 in tuition and fees.
"The fact that it was significantly cheaper than every other school made Bowdoin an easy decision for me," he said.

In North Carolina, Davidson College said earlier this year that families earning $175,000 or less will pay no tuition. Those making under $85,000 receive full scholarships covering tuition, fees, room and board. Families earning above $175,000 remain eligible based on calculated need.

There is a shrinking pool of high-school graduates and overall inflation is outpacing wage growth. That has pushed colleges to rethink who qualifies for relief, said Christopher Gruber, Davidson's vice president and dean of admission. "The competition has never been greater," he said.

Increasing financial aid generosity appears to be yielding results. Since Williams College announced its tuition-free policy for families making under $200,000 in 2022, applicants from the top two income quintiles have surged 20%, said Liz Creighton, the college's dean of admission and student financial services. She noted students are also working less hours at on-campus jobs and studying abroad in greater numbers since the policy's rollout.

The Education Department has also increased pressure on institutions to provide better economic value, enforcing rules that strip federal student-loan eligibility from certificate and career training programs whose graduates fail to meet minimum earnings benchmarks.

Carleton College in Minnesota recently announced it will eliminate loans from financial-aid packages starting next year. The move is part of an effort to ensure students aren't burdened by soaring debt or limited in their academic and career choices.

"What we're seeing is a market adjustment in liberal-arts colleges to stay viable in challenging financial times," said Nat Smitobol, an admissions counselor at IvyWise, a college admissions consulting firm. "Colleges are in a frenzy to pull any levers they can to maintain their numbers of applications."

Students apply for aid using the College Scholarship Service profile, an online application used by many selective colleges to award nonfederal institutional aid, alongside the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, or Fafsa.
Families with substantial assets, like a vacation home or a yacht, might not be eligible for full tuition assistance, even if their income falls below the college's threshold.

Sticker shock remains the one of the biggest deterrents for prospective liberal arts applicants, said Weingarten, at One-Stop College Counseling. Many families immediately balk at the price, unaware their kids can receive steep discounts.
But for those in the know, the discounts can be substantial.

Andre Culpepper-Wehr, 20, is the second child in his family to attend a liberal-arts college for its low cost. At Colby College in Maine, he received a scholarship that came with an academic stipend, alongside financial aid that covers his entire tuition. His sister graduated from Williams in 2024, which prompted him to also look at a liberal arts school, too.

"Being able to attend college and graduate debt-free opens up a lot of opportunities I wouldn't have been able to have otherwise considered," said Culpepper-Wehr, who will be interning at Goldman Sachs next summer.
